description: Matt's Deamon's is a team comprising of physicists and computer scientists who are excited to solve NASA's space app's challenge.
summary:
What did we develop?
The Mars EVA Traverse Board is an interactive route planner for astronauts on foot. It covers a patch of Gale crater, from the plains near Curiosity’s landing site to the base of Mount Sharp. The user drops a start pin and a destination pin. The board finds a walking route that avoids slopes of 20° or more and favours firm ground. It reports surface distance, suited walking time, climb, and an estimated radiation dose from cosmic rays and solar storms.

How it addresses the challenge?
The challenge asks for a layered, hyperlocal map built from several NASA missions. Ours combines five kinds of data: HiRISE imagery and terrain (optical and topographic), THEMIS thermal inertia (ground firmness), Curiosity RAD and REMS (radiation and atmosphere), and NOAA and NASA space weather. It puts them in one view that a crew could use to plan a single walk, with safety (slope and radiation) built into the route itself. Our geology objective is to reach both the plains rock and the Murray formation at Pahrump Hills.

Why it matters?
Existing tools show Mars at regional or global scale, but a crew needs one safe route for one excursion. Sending humans to Mars is NASA’s biggest challenge, and planning that walk from existing orbital and rover data is a practical step toward it. The approach could also be reused for lunar and other Mars sites.
details:
What it does and how it works

The user drops a start pin and a destination pin on a map of part of Gale crater. The board then:

  1. Finds a walking route with an A* search over a 5 m grid. Slopes of 20° or more are blocked, and the cost rises on steep ground, loose ground and high-radiation ground.
  2. Measures the route in 1.012 m steps, so climbs and descents count toward distance.
  3. Estimates suited walking time using Tobler’s hiking function, with an adjustable base speed of 3 km/h.
  4. Estimates the radiation dose for the walk from galactic cosmic rays and solar particles. The model accounts for the air overhead, the sky blocked by terrain, and suit shielding.
  5. Shows modelled pressure and temperature ranges, plus a snapshot of current space weather.

Benefits

  • The route is chosen for safety (slope, firm ground, dose), not just length.
  • The crew sees distance, time and dose before suiting up.
  • Every modelled or proxy value is labelled as such.

Intended impact

To show that existing NASA orbital and rover data can be layered into a planning tool for a single Marswalk. The same approach could extend to other Mars sites and, with lunar data, to the Moon.

Tools, languages and software

  • Python (route finding, coordinates, terrain processing, data building, space weather snapshots) and JavaScript with HTML for the interactive board.
  • QGIS for reprojecting, cropping and deriving slope.
  • Ruff, mypy in strict mode and ESLint for code quality.
  • Data: HiRISE imagery and terrain model (MRO), THEMIS (Mars Odyssey), Curiosity RAD and REMS, NOAA GOES, NASA DONKI, and the Oulu neutron monitor via NMDB.
  • Hardware: none beyond ordinary computers. Add anything else you used.

How it is creative

  • Radiation is part of the route cost, so the planner weighs dose along with slope and ground firmness.
  • Terrain shielding is modelled from a horizon scan, so crater walls and ridges reduce the dose.
  • Current space weather from Earth is scaled to a Mars dose estimate, using a published relationship.
  • The code follows NASA’s Power of 10 rules, with a 230-function audit.

Factors the team considered

  • Safety first: a hard slope limit, firm versus loose ground, and dose.
  • Suited mobility: slope-adjusted walking time at an assumed speed.
  • Honest data limits: weather is modelled, space weather is an Earth-based proxy, and the thermal data is coarse (100 m).
  • Model assumptions: the solar-particle attenuation length and quality factor are assumptions, and albedo neutrons are not modelled.
  • Speed versus checking: a route takes about 7 to 9 seconds because of the safety checks in the code.
